title: Ambiguity in Headlines and Slogans
text:
Advertisers and headline writers deliberately exploit ambiguity, since a phrase with two readings attracts attention more effectively than a plain statement. A slogan that suggests both a product's quality and a customer's status invites the audience to resolve the tension in their own favour. The effect depends on the audience sharing enough cultural knowledge to recognise both meanings at once.

Such devices can also mislead when one reading quietly displaces the other. A reader who notices only the flattering sense may absorb a claim the text never explicitly makes, while the literal meaning, which might be less favourable, slips away. Careful readers therefore ask which meaning the wording was designed to foreground and which it was designed to hide.

questions.text: According to the first paragraph, why do advertisers exploit ambiguity?
options: Because a phrase with two readings attracts attention more effectively

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, what can happen when one reading quietly displaces the other?
options: A reader may absorb a claim the text never explicitly makes
The product is withdrawn from sale
The slogan is translated into another language

questions.text: What does the passage imply about the effect of ambiguity on different readers?
options: It depends on the audience sharing enough cultural knowledge
It works equally well for every reader
It requires no cultural knowledge at all

questions.text: Why do careful readers ask which meaning the wording foregrounds?
options: To see which meaning was designed to be noticed and which to be hidden
To shorten the text for easier reading
To avoid reading the slogan altogether

vocabulary.definition: the quality of allowing more than one possible meaning
a short, memorable phrase used in advertising or campaigns
takes the place of something and pushes it out of its position
to make something prominent so that it is noticed first

paragraph_translations: Publicitários e autores de manchetes exploram deliberadamente a ambiguidade, pois uma frase com dois sentidos atrai a atenção com mais eficácia do que um enunciado simples. Um slogan que sugere ao mesmo tempo a qualidade de um produto e o status do cliente convida o público a resolver a tensão a seu favor. O efeito depende de o público compartilhar conhecimento cultural suficiente para reconhecer os dois sentidos de uma vez.

Esses recursos também podem enganar quando um sentido desloca discretamente o outro. Um leitor que percebe apenas o sentido lisonjeiro pode absorver uma afirmação que o texto nunca faz explicitamente, enquanto o sentido literal, talvez menos favorável, escapa. Leitores atentos, portanto, perguntam qual sentido a formulação foi concebida para ressaltar e qual foi concebida para ocultar.
